title: Migrating tool definitions from rules to MCP
body: As Cursor is supporting configuring project MCP servers with `<project-root>/.cursor/mcp.json`, any plans to migrate the tool definitions to MCP?
author: zhy3213

comments.body:
Yes, we've been thinking about and comparing it with MCP since Cursor supported it a month or two ago. Here are my thoughts:

1. The advantage of MCP is that it's more formalized and potentially easier to configure.
2. However, the downside is that it's harder for the average user to add new features and debug. Especially given our repository uses a combination of natural language and simple command lines to implement new agents, whereas MCP requires a formal Python project.
3. So, I don't see MCP as competing technology. It's mostly suited for different scenarios. If we aim to distribute mature software, we should use MCP. However, for quick prototyping, using natural language and simple command lines might be a better approach.

Therefore, my current inclination is to maintain our current process while keeping an eye on MCP. If it becomes an industry standard, we might need to transition to MCP. However, at this stage, MCP is still actively being developed; for example, it recently added a new `sampling` primitive. It might not be the right time to integrate it just yet.

This PR improves the handling and documentation of reasoning tokens across the codebase, with a focus on clarifying provider-specific behaviors and ensuring proper test coverage.

1. Documentation Improvements:
   - Added comprehensive docstrings explaining reasoning tokens in `TokenUsage` class

- Reasoning tokens are an o1-specific feature (OpenAI's most advanced model)

  - Anthropic: Has its own token tracking system

title: Use `uvx` to make the tools executable scripts
body: If you packaged and published the tools as scripts with `uv`, it would simplify the installation process and usage. The LLM could then just run `uvx web_scraper...` and not have to worry about dependencies
author: fmhall

comments.body: Yeah I think that's a great idea. I will try to do this change this week.

I'm not an uv expert, but after some research, I've got a few questions. As I understand it, `uvx` functions like temporary, implicit virtual environment management. It offers the convenience of not having to manually create or manage any virtual environments. However, if we're looking to do something more long-term, it may be better to explicitly manage a virtual environment using tools like `pip`, `uv`, or `poetry`.

So my current concern is more about balancing the initial setup convenience against the long-term maintainability. Given that our current approach works reasonably well and strikes a balance between these two aspects, I lean towards saying that `uv` is a superior all-in-one Python management tool in the doc. It's encouraged to use uv, but not to mandate it—especially with `uvx`. What do you think?

`uv` is definitely great. My initial thinking was that if you could do something like this:

Install flow:

1. Get `uv` if you don't have it already
2. Copy some rules files to your local

Thats actually it. Users don't even need to download the tools.

Then when the agent invokes the tools, they do so like: 
```bash
uvx llm_api --prompt "Your verification question" --provider {openai|anthropic} --image path/to/screenshot.png
```

And `uvx` handles the creation of the env in the background for them. Whereas with `uv` only, the users still need to install the tools.






> However, if we're looking to do something more long-term, it may be better to explicitly manage a virtual environment using tools like `pip`, `uv`, or `poetry`.

My understanding is that `uvx` does some seriously aggressive caching the first time it's called, which would essentially mean that once it's called the first time, it has slim to no overhead compared to the alternatives.

So you still get all the benefits of `uv`, but without the headache and friction of having to have that dedicated environment, since `uvx` is caching all that stuff behind the scenes. Plus, it's incredibly fast (go Rust!).

Either way, worth some experimentation, but I think you will be pleasantly surprised!
Merged the PR. Now we are using uv as the default package manager, and will fall back to pip when not installed.

# Improve LLM API Test Suite

Enhances the test suite to better handle LLM API configurations and failures, making it easier for contributors to understand why tests are skipped or failing.

## Changes

1. Add smart API key validation
   - Detect unconfigured or example API keys from .env.example
   - Skip tests appropriately with informative messages
   - Centralize key validation logic in test_utils.py

2. Improve live test reliability
   - Add graceful error handling for API failures
   - Convert API errors to skipped tests rather than failures
   - Consolidate response assertions into helper method

3. Better developer experience
   - Update README to document verbose test output
   - Add clear messages about why tests were skipped
   - Clean up duplicate code in test files

## Testing
Verified by running test suite with:
- No .env file (tests properly skipped)
- .env with example values (tests properly skipped)
- .env with invalid API keys (graceful error handling)
- .env with valid API keys (tests pass)

## Usage
Run tests with:
```bash
PYTHONPATH=. pytest -v tests/
```
The `-v` flag shows detailed output including why tests were skipped.

title: How to check whether Cursor actually uses the cursor rules file?
body:
Hi Yan,

I replaced the locally deployed llm by openai api, and passed all the tests, meaning all the tools are available and can be invoked properly. While when I ask Cursor composer/agent or chat whether you have to load cursorrules file before actually executing any tasks, it said no. Afterwards,  I ran several tasks with the agent mode and checked my open ai api usage, there's no request coming from Cursor, however, it is not a objective and definitive way to tell whether this high level instruction is loaded. Wondering whether you have experience on this issue and if it doesn't load, how to fix it.

Best,
Weixian
author: weixiandeng

comments.body:
I used a smart trick to tell whether the cursor rules are used or not. I include a prompt such as "always begin and end your answer with ***" and then check if the cursor follows this format. I've tried this in various scenarios, and it always seemed to work with previous versions of the cursor, specifically before version 0.44. However, with the different variants of version 0.44, this behavior has become inconsistent. In version 0.44, I often manually add the cursor rules into the context window, which kind of defeats the purpose of this file. I'm also curious about how to restore the old behavior.

But another observation is: in my `.cursorrules`, I mentioned there is a virtual environment. Sometimes, Cursor would use the system's default Python, ignoring this instruction, which may hint that the `.cursorrules` were not included in the context window. However, after the first error, it knows to invoke the correct venv. So I guess at some point, the `.cursorrules` were then reintroduced in the context window. I'm just not clear about when that moment is.

I noticed similar behavior, like it actually activated the venv, but seems it doesn't really use the tools. Then I tried asking it to read cursor rules file before execution and it did invoke tools while it doesn't do sub-tasks nor add any learned lessons.

I had a similar observation, but in my case, I found that the tools is relatively fine. It is able to still use the tools when asked about relevant tasks, but it seems to be more reluctant to update the cursor rules, unless specifically told to do so. (like "take notes on your leanings").

Using .vscode/settings.json in a project can guide the editor to a specific virtual environment (venv) by configuring the setting "python.defaultInterpreterPath". However, if the project is opened before the venv is created, Cursor (VSCode) may report an issue with selecting an invalid interpreter.

.vscode/settings.json
```
{
    "python.defaultInterpreterPath": "./venv/bin/python"
}
```

Closing due to lack of activity. But feel free to reopen.

@yelban Sorry I just saw this message. I would recommend to create a separate issue for further discussion if you think the experience is bad.
